caption:
More than 500 Google workers signed a petition against the company's school Search policy.
Right now, schools that switch off AI lose Google Search too.
The workers warn schools may drop Google products altogether.

Should schools be able to use Google Search with no AI at all?

threads_text: Google's own employees are pushing back: more than 500 signed a petition asking the company to let schools keep Search without the AI features. Today it is all or nothing. Should schools get Google Search with the AI switched off?

slides.headline: Google's own workers tell the company to stop forcing AI on schools that just want *Search*

site_article.headline: Google employees petition the company to offer schools Search without AI
site_article.dek: More than 500 workers backed a letter from the Alphabet Workers Union asking Google to stop tying school access to Search to its AI features.
site_article.summary: More than 500 Google employees signed a petition asking the company to let K-12 schools use Search with its AI features switched off. Under a policy Google set in November 2026, schools that disable AI also lose access to Search.
site_article.seo_title: Google workers petition for school Search without AI
site_article.seo_description: More than 500 Google employees signed a petition asking the company to let K-12 schools use Google Search with AI Overviews and Gemini features turned off.
site_article.answer_summary: Google employees organized by the Alphabet Workers Union want schools to be able to use Google Search without its AI features. Under Google's current policy, schools that turn AI off lose Search as well.
site_article.hero_alt: Protesters holding signs outside a Google office building in Chicago.

paragraphs.text: More than 500 Google employees have signed a petition asking the company to let schools use Google Search without its AI features, according to a statement released on November 19, 2026, by members of the Alphabet Workers Union, CWA Local 9009, Engadget reported. Bloomberg, as cited by The Next Web, put the count at more than 540 employees and contractors.

The letter was addressed to chief executive Sundar Pichai, Search head Elizabeth Reid and education chief Chris Phillips, according to The Next Web. The workers asked leadership to reconsider the policy and to allow schools to disable AI features in Search without disrupting their ability to use Search as a whole, Engadget reported.

The signers argued that cutting off Search for schools that do not want AI will not win over users and is more likely to push them away from Google products altogether, according to both outlets. Google did not immediately comment to Bloomberg, The Next Web reported.

Earlier in November, Google said it would switch off Gemini and Search for K-12 student accounts unless schools turn them on, according to The Next Web. Because AI is built into Search, a school that turns Search back on also gets its AI features, which leaves schools that want no AI at all without Google Search. Engadget reported that Google framed the decision around Search and AI being deeply integrated.

School districts in New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are considering an alternative search engine, Engadget reported, citing The New York Times. A Chicago Public Schools spokesperson told Chalkbeat the district was exploring ways to suppress the AI overview on its own and would look to other search options if it could not offer students Search without AI.

On November 11, about 30 parents, students and school board members gathered outside Google's office in Chicago's West Loop in a rally led by Illinois Families for Public Schools, Chalkbeat reported. A Google spokesperson told Chalkbeat the company is taking steps to improve Search for classrooms, including a pilot of its Guided Learning feature, which uses AI to walk students through problems step by step.

Sen. Ed Markey wrote to Google on November 9 asking whether schools could keep Search with AI switched off, and Common Sense Media described Google's AI Search as an unacceptable risk for students in July, according to The Next Web. The outlet also noted that Chrome OS ran on 58 percent of laptops and tablets shipped to US schools last year, citing Futuresource Consulting.

Dan Carroll, co-founder of the education technology company Clever, described the situation as a real strategic pickle for districts, according to The Next Web, because Chromebooks are built around Google's software and changing search engines takes time and training. The Alphabet Workers Union previously organized staff over job security in July, according to The Next Web.

The petition adds an internal voice to a dispute that had been driven by parents, districts and lawmakers. Google's position rests on the idea that Search and AI can no longer be separated, while its own employees are arguing that the all or nothing approach risks losing a market where its hardware and software are already standard.
The key signal is whether Google offers K-12 accounts a Search setting without AI features, or whether New York City, Los Angeles or Chicago formally switch to another search engine.
